title: Neural, LLM and Agentic POS Tagging
oneLiner: How tagging moved from counting tables to neural networks, giant pre-trained models, simple prompts and AI agents that call a tagger as a tool.

what.html:
Modern taggers climb a ladder. First, turn words into vectors. Then read the sentence in both directions with a memory network and choose a sensible tag sequence (Bi-LSTM-CRF). Then let every word look at every other word at once (Transformers), starting from a model that already knows language (BERT). Finally, simply ask a large language model, or let an AI agent call a tagger when it needs one.

Everyday versionA word is like a person with several possible jobs: "coach" can be a bus, a trainer or the act of training. You tell which from the company it keeps, and each rung of the ladder lets the model see more of that company.

why.html:
• Accuracy rose from about 90% (no context) to about 99%.
  • The same ladder describes how almost every NLP task modernised.
  • Today tagging is often one quiet step inside bigger AI systems.

how.title: Start from the dumbest tagger
how.html: Give each word its most common tag. "She books a flight" goes wrong on "books" (usually a plural noun), the one word that matters.

how.title: Words as vectors, plus spelling
how.html: Similar words get similar vectors (king and queen: cosine 0.996). For unseen words, spelling clues like "-ly" or "-ing" still give useful evidence.

how.title: Read with a memory, both ways
how.html: An LSTM reads word by word with three dials: how much old memory to keep, how much new to write, how much to read out. Running one forward and one backward lets each word see both sides.

how.title: Choose tags that fit together
how.html: For "the plays", the verb reading of "plays" scores higher alone, but "determiner then noun" is so natural that the whole-sequence winner is DT NN (97.5%).

how.title: Why the last percent matters
how.html: At 97% per word, only about 54% of 20-word sentences are perfect; at 99%, about 82%.

how.title: Every word looks at every word
how.html: Self-attention lets "bank" put 81% of its attention on "river" directly, however far away it is, giving a strong noun signal.

how.title: Start from a model that already knows English
how.html: Fine-tune BERT with one small layer on top of each word's vector: for "she plays well" it says verb with 77% confidence. Tag only the first piece of a split word.

how.title: Just ask
how.html: Ask a chatbot to tag with Penn tags. Without examples it may say "ADJ" instead of "JJ"; two examples in the prompt fix the format.

how.title: Tagging as a tool
how.html: An AI agent asked for "sentiment of all nouns in reviews" plans the job, calls a fast tagger to find the nouns, then reports battery +0.8, screen −0.6.

demo.html: Match each description to its rung on the ladder, from the lookup table to the tool-using agent.

example.html:
Scoring "the plays". Determiner for "the" (5) + reward for determiner→noun (4) + noun for "plays" (2) = 11. The greedy choice determiner→verb gives 5 − 1 + 3 = 7. After exponentiating and normalising over all nine options, DT NN gets 97.5%.

Supplementary Benchmarks use tidy newspaper text. On social-media posts or mixed-language messages, accuracy can drop by several points, so always test on your own kind of text.

misunderstandings: 97% means almost every sentence is right.
They show what was looked at; later layers decide.
For volume and consistency, fine-tuned models win.
They call a tagger as a tool.
takeaways: Each rung uses more context: baseline → HMM/CRF → Bi-LSTM-CRF → Transformer → prompting → agents.
LSTM gates; Bi-LSTM reads both ways; CRF picks consistent sequences.
aⁿ: small per-token gains matter at sentence level.
Fine-tuned Transformers ≈ 99%; prompts need examples; agents call tools.
thirty: The unigram baseline (~90%) ignores context (She books → NNS, wrong). Word embeddings make similar words close (king–queen 0.996, king–cat −0.135); character embeddings handle OOV words. LSTMs gate memory (worked c = 0.763, h = 0.422); Bi-LSTMs read both ways. A CRF scores sequences Σ E + Σ T and normalises by Z: 'the plays' DT NN = 11 vs greedy DT VBZ = 7, P = 0.975. Bi-LSTM-CRF ≈ 97–98%; 0.97²⁰ ≈ 0.544 vs 0.99²⁰ ≈ 0.818. Self-attention softmax(q·k/√d) puts 0.807 on 'river' for 'bank'. Fine-tuned BERT adds a linear head (plays → VBZ 0.773), tags the first subword, reaches ≈ 99%. Zero-shot prompts may use the wrong tagset; few-shot fixes it. Agents call a tagger tool inside larger tasks (battery +0.8, screen −0.6).
